docs.title: E04 · Frozen foundation models + decoder (RQ1)
docs.text:
Status: planned (Morocco first, Utah later)

Same labelled pixels and tiles as E03 (Morocco 2023/24 and 2024/25 pooled, 473,675 pixels in 2,015 tiles; two classes); six encoders, one GPU job each, 3 seeds per round. Code ready and tested (Prithvi); results follow after the runs.

Question (RQ1). Do frozen geospatial foundation models with a light decoder classify the pixels better than the pixel models (E01, E02) and a spatio-temporal network trained from scratch (E03)? (Answered on the comparison page.)

What changes from E03. The image encoder: a pretrained, frozen foundation model instead of a convolutional encoder trained from scratch. Tiles, labelled pixels, loss, training and metrics are the same.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
The encoders see whole 128 × 128 px tiles; the model predicts every pixel and is scored at the labelled pixels of the pixel samples.

flowchart TD A[128 px tile, 12 months] --> B[Frozen encoder, per month] B --> C[L-TAE over months, per patch] C --> D[Feature pyramid + UPerNet] D --> E[Class per 10 m pixel] Encoder Bands Months per pass Patch Feature size Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M-TL B2 B3 B4 B8A B11 B12 4, with date and location 16 px 1024 Clay v1.5 10 bands (no B1, B9) 1, with week and location 8 px 1024 TerraMind 1.0 base 12 bands (S2L2A) 1 16 px 768 AgriFM 10 bands all 12 (time merged inside the model) 4 px, pyramid to 32 px multi-scale Presto 10 bands + NDVI all 12 (per pixel, inside the model) 1 pixel 128 per pixel TESSERA v2 Medium 10 bands the clear months, dated by day of year (per pixel) 1 pixel 128 per pixel

All six encoders are loaded by pixelwise_run/encoders.py with the band order, normalisation and weights of their pretraining (the four image models exactly as in the archived embedding scripts); AgriFM is normalised with the region's band statistics, Presto and TESSERA with their own input scaling. The two pixel models encode every pixel of the tile, so their output is already a 10 m feature map (D15). Details of the models: Foundation models.

Part Choice Temporal head L-TAE (16 heads, dk 8, dmodel 256, output 256) over the 12 months at every patch position; months without a clear pixel in the patch are masked. AgriFM, Presto, TESSERA: none (the encoder handles time) Decoder 4-scale feature pyramid from the single-scale ViT features (×4, ×2, ×1, ×½, as for plain ViTs in PANGAEA; Marsocci et al. 2024) and a UPerNet head (Xiao et al. 2018; pool sizes 1, 2, 4), upsampled to 10 m. AgriFM: its own 4-level pyramid goes straight into the UPerNet head. Presto, TESSERA: the 10 m map average-pooled to 4 scales (×1, ×½, ×¼, ×⅛) Output 2 class scores (irrigated, rainfed) on a 32 × 32 grid, upsampled to every 10 m pixel Trained temporal head and decoder only (about 2.4–3.2 M weights); the encoder stays frozen in evaluation mode What \"frozen encoder\" means

A foundation model has been pretrained once, without labels, on millions of images. Its encoder turns an image into features. Frozen means its weights are not changed at all during our training: it is used as a fixed feature extractor, in evaluation mode (no dropout, no updates). Only the small head after it (L-TAE, feature pyramid, UPerNet) learns from our labels. E04 therefore measures what the pretrained features already contain for irrigated / rainfed. Training the encoder as well is RQ2 (E05).

The six encoders in one paragraph each
  • Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M (NASA, IBM): a vision transformer (24 blocks) pretrained by masked-autoencoding on Landsat-Sentinel-2 (HLS) time series; reads 4 months per pass with their dates and the location, one vector per 16 × 16 px patch.
  • Clay v1.5: a vision transformer that encodes each band with its wavelength, so one model reads many sensors; one month per pass, 8 × 8 px patches.
  • TerraMind 1.0 base (IBM, ESA): a multimodal model pretrained to generate any of nine modalities from the others; here Sentinel-2 only, one month per pass, 16 × 16 px patches.
  • AgriFM: a video-Swin transformer pretrained for agricultural mapping; reads all 12 months at once and returns its own four-level feature pyramid.
  • Presto (NASA Harvest): a small transformer over the time series of one pixel (0.4 M weights); every pixel of the tile is encoded on its own into a 128-value vector.
  • TESSERA v2: a per-pixel model trained so that its 128-value embedding does not depend on which cloud-free dates were available (summary).

Bands, normalisation and weights of each model: Foundation models.

How the feature pyramid works

A plain vision transformer returns a single map (for Prithvi 8 × 8 per tile), but UPerNet needs four resolutions. The pyramid rescales that one map to four sizes: ×4 (32 × 32) with two learnt 2 × 2 transposed convolutions, ×2 (16 × 16) with one, ×1 (8 × 8) with a 1 × 1 convolution, ×½ (4 × 4) with max pooling. The scales and operations follow the Feature2Pyramid neck of PANGAEA and MMSegmentation; building all four from the last encoder layer only follows ViTDet (Li et al. 2022). The upsampled maps are learnt, not new detail: the true resolution stays the 16 px patch. AgriFM gives its own pyramid; for Presto and TESSERA the 10 m feature map is average-pooled to four sizes.

How L-TAE combines the months

For the encoders that read one month (or four months) per pass, the twelve monthly feature vectors of each patch are combined by an L-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2020): 16 heads each give the months weights that sum to 1 (months without a clear pixel in the patch get weight 0) and average them; the result is one 256-value vector per patch. Details: E03 · How L-TAE works.

How UPerNet works (the decoder)

The encoder describes the tile in coarse blocks: for Prithvi one vector per 16 × 16 px patch, an 8 × 8 grid for a 128 px tile. UPerNet (Xiao et al. 2018) turns these coarse features into a class for every pixel. It does so by looking at the tile at several sizes at once: coarse maps carry the context (what kind of landscape is this?), finer maps carry the position (where does the field end?).

flowchart LR A["encoder features<br/>8 × 8 per tile"] --> B["pyramid: 4 sizes<br/>32², 16², 8², 4²"] B --> C["1 · context:<br/>average the coarsest map<br/>over the whole tile, its halves<br/>and quarters"] C --> D["2 · coarse to fine:<br/>upsample, add the next<br/>finer map, smooth"] D --> E["3 · combine the 4 sizes,<br/>classify"] E --> F["class per pixel<br/>(32 × 32, then 128 × 128)"]
  1. Pyramid. A plain vision transformer gives only one map size, so the 8 × 8 map is rescaled to four sizes (32 × 32, 16 × 16, 8 × 8, 4 × 4).
  2. Context. On the coarsest map, the features are averaged over the whole tile, over 2 × 2 and over 4 × 4 regions, and added back to every position, so each position also "knows" its surroundings (an irrigation scheme or a dry plain).
  3. From coarse to fine. Starting from the coarsest map, each step doubles the size and adds the next finer map, so the context flows down into the detailed maps.
  4. Combine and classify. The four maps are brought to 32 × 32 (40 m), joined, and a final layer gives two scores per position (irrigated, rainfed); they are then upsampled to 128 × 128, i.e. to every 10 m pixel.

What it can and cannot do. UPerNet adds spatial context, which helps where a single pixel is ambiguous. It cannot add detail the encoder does not have: all four sizes come from the same 16 px patches, so field edges stay soft. UPerNet is the standard decoder of the PANGAEA benchmark (Marsocci et al. 2024) and is the same for every encoder, so it does not favour any of them.

docs.title: E05 · Prithvi: frozen, LoRA, fine-tuned, from scratch
E05 · Prithvi: frozen, LoRA, fine-tuned or from scratch (RQ2)
docs.text:
Status: planned (Morocco first, Utah later)

Code: experiments/E05_prithvi_strategies/ and pixelwise_run/tile_common.py, ready and tested. Same labelled pixels as E01–E04: Morocco 2023/24 and 2024/25 pooled, 473,675 pixels in 2,015 tiles (7,579 irrigated and 1,196 rainfed parcels), two classes. 16 GPU jobs: 4 strategies × 4 label shares.

Questions.

  1. How do the four ways of training the same network behave: speed of learning, overfitting, stability?
  2. What does training the encoder (a few adapter weights or every weight) cost (trained weights, GPU time) and what does it change compared with the frozen encoder of E04?
  3. Does full fine-tuning beat the frozen encoder and the same network trained from scratch, does parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) keep the gain at a fraction of the trained weights, and do the answers depend on the number of labelled parcels?

What changes from E04. Only the encoder: whether it starts from the pretrained weights and whether its weights are trained (none, low-rank adapters, or all). Network, tiles, labelled pixels, folds, loss and metrics are those of E04, so the four strategies differ in nothing else. A fourth factor, the share of training parcels (10, 25, 50, 100%), shows where pretraining pays off. Prithvi is the only encoder: it is the model of the study that motivated E05 (below), a plain ViT whose architecture TerraTorch builds with random weights as easily as with pretrained ones, and the GeoFM for which LoRA has been compared with full fine-tuning (Marti-Escofet et al. 2025). One encoder keeps the cost at 16 jobs.

The question follows a recent study that fine-tuned Prithvi-EO-2.0 for crop-type mapping of smallholder farms (Tomotaki-Dawoud et al. 2025): full fine-tuning gave a macro-F1 of 0.79 against 0.56 for the frozen encoder and 0.63 from scratch. That study used one validation split, no confidence intervals, three dates of 30 m HLS imagery resampled to 0.5 m, and 601 parcels. E05 repeats the comparison with spatial cross-validation, block-bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests, 12 monthly composites of 10 m Sentinel-2, and a label-share curve. LoRA is added because, for Prithvi-EO-2.0 on five segmentation tasks, it matched full fine-tuning with 1.8% of the encoder's weights trained and generalised better to held-out regions (Marti-Escofet et al. 2025).

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
The same network in every run (GeoFMSegmenter in tile_common.py, as in E04):

flowchart TD A["128 × 128 px tile · 12 months · 6 bands (B2 B3 B4 B8A B11 B12)"] --> B["Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M encoder: 24 transformer blocks, 16 px patches, 4 months per pass with date and location"] B --> C["Output of the last block: 8 × 8 patch grid × 1024 values, per month"] C --> D["L-TAE over the 12 months at each patch position → 256 values"] D --> E["Feature pyramid ×4 ×2 ×1 ×½ → 32², 16², 8², 4²"] E --> F["UPerNet head → class scores on 32 × 32 (40 m)"] F --> G["Bilinear to 128 × 128 → irrigated / rainfed per 10 m pixel"] Part Choice Source Encoder Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M-TL: ViT-Large, 24 blocks, 1024-d tokens, 16 px patches; 4 months per pass with temporal and location encodings; the 12 months in three passes. Bands and normalisation of the model card Szwarcman et al. (2024) Encoder output tokens of the last block, without the class token: an 8 × 8 grid per month single-scale design of ViTDet (Li et al. 2022) Temporal head L-TAE over the 12 months at each of the 64 patch positions (16 heads, dk 8, dmodel 256, output 256); months without a clear pixel in the patch are masked Garnot & Landrieu (2020); multi-temporal set-up of PANGAEA (Marsocci et al. 2024) Feature pyramid ×4: two 2 × 2 transposed convolutions (GroupNorm, GELU between); ×2: one transposed convolution; ×1: 1 × 1 convolution; ×½: 2 × 2 max-pooling + 1 × 1 convolution; 128 channels the Feature2Pyramid neck that PANGAEA uses for ViT encoders (from MMSegmentation, used with BEiT and MAE); ViTDet Decoder UPerNet: pyramid pooling (1, 2, 4) on the coarsest map, top-down feature pyramid, fusion of the four levels, dropout 0.1, 1 × 1 classifier (2 classes); then bilinear upsampling to 10 m Xiao et al. (2018); PANGAEA Head size 2.48 M weights (L-TAE + pyramid + UPerNet), newly initialised in every run E04 Why the pyramid is built from one layer

A plain ViT returns one map at one resolution (one vector per 16 px patch), but UPerNet combines several resolutions. PANGAEA (Feature2Pyramid, with the scales 4, 2, 1, ½) and the MMSegmentation configurations for BEiT and MAE rescale four different encoder layers (for a 12-block ViT, blocks 4, 6, 8 and 12). ViTDet showed that a pyramid rescaled from the last layer alone is sufficient (Li et al. 2022); E04 and E05 use this simpler form, which needs one L-TAE instead of four. All four maps have the same true resolution (16 px): the ×4 and ×2 maps are learnt upsamplings, so the decision grid is 40 m and field edges are soft. The head is identical in the four strategies, so this choice does not favour any of them. How UPerNet works: E04.

docs.title: The four strategies
docs.text:
flowchart LR P["Pretrained Prithvi weights"] --> FR["Frozen: encoder locked, head trained"] P --> LO["LoRA: encoder locked, low-rank adapters and head trained"] P --> FT["Full fine-tuning: encoder and head trained, encoder at 1/10 of the head's learning rate"] R["Random weights, same architecture"] --> SC["From scratch: encoder and head trained, same learning rate"] Frozen LoRA Full fine-tuning From scratch Encoder starts from pretrained weights pretrained weights pretrained weights random weights (TerraTorch initialisation, seeded per run) Encoder trained no (evaluation mode, no gradients) no; adapters added to the attention (qkv) and MLP (fc1, fc2) layers of all 24 blocks are trained (training mode) yes (training mode) yes (training mode) Head trained yes yes yes yes Trained weights ≈ 2.5 M ≈ 8.0 M (5.5 M adapters + 2.5 M head) ≈ 306 M ≈ 306 M Learning rate head 10⁻⁴ head and adapters 10⁻⁴ head 10⁻⁴, encoder 10⁻⁵ head and encoder 10⁻⁴ Best model kept head head + adapters head + encoder head + encoder What it measures what the pretrained features hold for the task how much a small, low-rank change of the encoder adds what adapting every feature adds what the network learns without pretraining Frozen

Frozen is E04 for Prithvi. The encoder describes each patch as it learnt in pretraining; the head learns to read these descriptions. It cannot add a distinction the pretrained features do not contain.

Full fine-tuning

Full fine-tuning starts from the same weights but lets the error of the labels flow back into all 24 blocks, so the features themselves move towards irrigated / rainfed. The encoder gets a ten times smaller learning rate than the new head: the head starts from random weights and must learn fast, the encoder should only shift. Different learning rates for different parts of a pretrained network are the "discriminative fine-tuning" of Howard & Ruder (2018), here in its simplest two-group form. A large step on a pretrained encoder can distort the pretrained features and generalise worse to data unlike the training data (Kumar et al. 2022), which matters for the year-transfer test (RQ3).

LoRA (low-rank adaptation)

LoRA (Hu et al. 2021) keeps every pretrained weight fixed and adds, next to each adapted linear layer W, a trainable update B·A of rank 16 (A: 16 × input size, B: output size × 16; output W x + (α/r) B A x with α = 32). B starts at zero, so training starts exactly from the pretrained network, as in full fine-tuning; but the change of each layer is limited to 16 directions. The adapted layers and the rank follow Marti-Escofet et al. (2025), who used rank 16 on the attention and feed-forward layers of Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M (about 5.5 M weights, 1.8% of the encoder; Prithvi's query, key and value share one qkv layer, which is adapted as a whole). Memory stays close to the frozen run: no gradients or optimiser states for the 304 M encoder weights. Diagram: RQ2 · Fine-tuning.

From scratch

The same 300 M network with random weights, trained like the fine-tuned one (encoder and head at 10⁻⁴). The difference to full fine-tuning is the starting point only, so it isolates the value of pretraining. A ViT-Large has far more weights than a few thousand parcels can determine; it is expected to be the weakest at small label shares. It is a reference for this network, not the best model trained from scratch: that is U-TAE (E03, 1.15 M weights).

docs.title: Fewer labels
docs.text:
Only the training folds are thinned; the validation and test folds are always complete.

flowchart TD A["5 spatial folds (20 km blocks)"] --> B["Round k of 5: 3 training folds · 1 validation fold · 1 test fold"] B --> C["Training-fold parcels: keep 10 / 25 / 50 / 100 % per class (fixed random order, nested)"] C --> D["Kept parcels: labels in the loss · dropped parcels: pixels stay in the image, unlabelled"] D --> F["Training tiles = tiles with a kept label"] B --> G["Validation fold: all parcels → early stopping"] B --> H["Test fold: all parcels → out-of-fold prediction"] Item Rule Unit the parcel (all its sampled pixels together), the unit a field survey delivers Draw every parcel gets one fixed random number (seed 7); per class the training parcels with the smallest numbers are kept, so the class shares stay as in the full set and the 10% set lies inside the 25% set, and so on Same for all strategies the four strategies see the same parcels at each share Validation, test unchanged; every run predicts all 473,675 pixels once (out of fold), so all 16 runs are scored on the same pixels and can be compared pairwise Validation stays complete early stopping uses the full validation fold at every share. With only 10% of the labels a real project would also have less validation data, so the low-share scores are slightly optimistic for all four strategies alike

Labelled training data per round (Morocco, mean of the five rounds; label_subset.csv of each run):

Share Irrigated parcels Rainfed parcels Irrigated pixels Rainfed pixels Training tiles 10% 455 72 25,307 3,530 436 25% 1,137 180 62,117 8,212 740 50% 2,274 359 126,876 16,195 987 100% 4,547 718 251,930 32,275 1,232

At 10% only about 72 rainfed parcels per round remain: the low end of the curve shows how the strategies cope with a few dozen examples of the minority class.

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
Identical for the four strategies except the learning rates above:

Item Choice Labels labelled pixels of the round's training folds (of the kept parcels); all other pixels ignored in the loss Loss class-weighted cross-entropy (weights from the kept training pixels) Optimiser AdamW, weight decay 10⁻⁴, batch 8 tiles, bfloat16 mixed precision Warm-up learning rate rises linearly over the first epoch, then constant (Goyal et al. 2017); avoids large first steps on the randomly initialised head and encoder Gradient clipping total gradient norm ≤ 1 Augmentation random flips and 90° rotations Early stopping macro-F1 of the validation pixels; patience 15, at most 60 epochs (E04: 8 and 50; longer here so that the curves show the overfitting phase) Seeds 3 per round (42, 1042, 2042), mean probability; the seed also sets the initial weights of the head, of the LoRA adapters and, from scratch, of the encoder Logged per epoch training loss, validation loss (the same weighted cross-entropy), validation macro-F1 and rainfed F1, seconds

The frozen run at 100% repeats E04 Prithvi with a longer patience, warm-up and gradient clipping; its score should lie close to E04's and is a check of the code.

Settings not tuned: the learning rates (10⁻⁴ is E04's; 10⁻⁵ for the encoder is the tenfold reduction; the LoRA adapters use the head's 10⁻⁴, since they start at zero and are small), the LoRA rank, weight decay and the head. They are the same for every share.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
flowchart LR J["16 jobs: 4 strategies × 4 shares"] --> R["each: 5 rounds × 3 seeds"] R --> O["out-of-fold predictions of all pixels, metrics with CI, training history"] O --> S["report.py"] S --> T1["summary.csv: scores, trained weights, epochs, time"] S --> T2["paired.csv: paired tests per share"] S --> F1["learning curves"] S --> F2["score vs share of parcels"] S --> F3["confusion matrices at 100%"] Question Evidence 1. How the strategies behave training and validation loss and validation macro-F1 per epoch (100% of the labels; mean over the 15 runs, band = range): speed of learning, gap between training and validation loss, epoch of the best model 2. What fine-tuning costs and changes trained weights, seconds per epoch, GPU hours; fine-tuned − frozen and LoRA − frozen at each share; confusion matrices (does it reduce the rainfed → irrigated confusion?) 3. Whether fine-tuning wins paired block-bootstrap differences on the same pixels at each share: fine-tuned − frozen (effect of training the encoder), fine-tuned − scratch (effect of the pretrained weights), frozen − scratch, LoRA − frozen (effect of the adapters), fine-tuned − LoRA (full against parameter-efficient fine-tuning), LoRA − scratch. Holm correction per metric over the 24 comparisons (6 pairs × 4 shares); a difference counts when its 95% CI excludes 0 and pHolm < 0.05 (as in E01–E04). Score against share of parcels with E03 U-TAE and E01 random forest at 100% as reference lines

Headline metric: macro-F1 of irrigated and rainfed; rainfed F1, precision and recall also reported. E05 is compared within itself; 05_compare_experiments.py compares E01–E04 only.

docs.title: How to run
docs.text:
Script: experiments/E05_prithvi_strategies/run.py (settings at the top; strategy and share from EXPERIMENT_STRATEGY and EXPERIMENT_FRACTION). One GPU job per strategy and share; needs the Morocco tile store outputs/morocco/dataset/03_tiles_128px/agyear/tiles/, the pixel samples outputs/morocco/dataset/04_pixel_samples/ and the Prithvi weights in checkpoints/prithvi/.

Quick test first, one per strategy (60 tiles, 2 epochs, 1 seed; too short to learn the rainfed class, it reads the epoch time and GPU memory):

for s in frozen lora finetune scratch; do sbatch --export=ALL,SCRIPT=experiments/E05_prithvi_strategies/run.py,EXPERIMENT_REGION=morocco,EXPERIMENT_STRATEGY=$s,EXPERIMENT_FRACTION=0.5,EXPERIMENT_QUICK_TEST=1 jobs/step_gpu.sbatch; done

Then the 16 runs:

for s in frozen lora finetune scratch; do for f in 0.1 0.25 0.5 1.0; do sbatch --time=72:00:00 --export=ALL,SCRIPT=experiments/E05_prithvi_strategies/run.py,EXPERIMENT_REGION=morocco,EXPERIMENT_STRATEGY=$s,EXPERIMENT_FRACTION=$f jobs/step_gpu.sbatch; done; done

After copying results/ to the Mac (report.py uses whatever runs are finished):

python experiments/E05_prithvi_strategies/report.py

Compute (estimate, to be replaced by the quick-test times). Frozen Prithvi took about 75 s per epoch on the Morocco tiles in the earlier runs. Fine-tuning and training from scratch also run the backward pass through the 300 M encoder: in local tests about 1.8 (fine-tuning) and 2.4 (from scratch) times the frozen time per epoch; LoRA about 1.3 times. With the longer patience, roughly 140 GPU hours for the 16 jobs.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: experiments/E05_prithvi_strategies/results/morocco/<strategy>_p<share>/ (e.g. finetune_p025/, lora_p100/): the E01 files plus training_history.csv (per epoch: training loss, validation loss, validation macro-F1 and rainfed F1, seconds) and label_subset.csv (parcels, pixels and tiles kept per round, for shares below 100%). report.py writes results/morocco/summary.csv, results/morocco/paired.csv and the figures e05_curves.png, e05_label_fraction.png and e05_confusion.png in docs/experiments/figures/.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• One encoder, and Morocco first (Utah follows). Prithvi is pretrained on 30 m HLS and here receives 10 m Sentinel-2, so its frozen features meet a different pixel size than in pretraining; fine-tuning may gain more for Prithvi than for an encoder pretrained on Sentinel-2 at 10 m.
  • No search over learning rates per strategy, nor over the LoRA rank and adapted layers: a strategy may be favoured by settings that suit it better (Marti-Escofet et al. 2025 chose the learning rate of each method by a search).
  • The validation fold is complete at every share (see above).
  • Other parameter-efficient methods (adapters, prompt tuning) and two-stage linear probing then fine-tuning (LP-FT) are not compared (RQ2 · Fine-tuning).

docs.title: Comparison of the experiments
docs.text:
Status: Morocco E01 and E02 done; E03 and E04 running (Utah later)

This page holds all runs of E01–E04 side by side as they finish. Each experiment page reports only its own runs; E05 (Prithvi frozen / LoRA / fine-tuned / from scratch) is compared within itself on its own page.

docs.title: What will be compared
docs.text:
All runs of a region are scored on the same out-of-fold pixels: Morocco 2023/24 and 2024/25 pooled, 473,675 labelled pixels of 8,775 surveyed parcels, two classes (irrigated, rainfed).

Run Experiment Model E01 random forest E01 pixel time series, random forest (reference) E01 gradient boosting E01 pixel time series, histogram gradient boosting E02 TempCNN E02 pixel time series, temporal CNN E03 U-TAE E03 whole tiles, trained from scratch (reference for E04) E04 Prithvi, Clay, TerraMind, AgriFM, Presto, TESSERA E04 whole tiles, frozen foundation model + L-TAE + UPerNet

docs.title: Planned tables and figures
docs.text:
Content How Scores macro-F1 (irrigated, rainfed; headline), rainfed F1, precision and recall, with 95% block-bootstrap CI Paired tests against the E01 random forest does a model beat the pixel baseline? Difference on the same pixels, 95% CI, Holm-corrected p Paired tests against E03 U-TAE does pretraining add anything beyond the spatial context of the tile? Figures scores of all runs with CIs; confusion matrices of the random forest, U-TAE and the best foundation model

A difference counts when its 95% CI excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p < 0.05 (evaluation protocol). Tables and tests: pixelwise_run/05_compare_experiments.py (experiments/comparison/<region>/); figures: experiments/report_figures.py (docs/experiments/figures/).

docs.title: Morocco (finished runs so far)
docs.text:
Run Macro-F1 [95% CI] Rainfed F1 [95% CI] Δ macro-F1 vs E01 random forest [95% CI] Holm-adjusted p E01 random forest (reference) 0.894 [0.834, 0.940] 0.810 [0.697, 0.894] – – E01 gradient boosting 0.893 [0.822, 0.946] 0.809 [0.673, 0.903] −0.000 [−0.017, +0.014] 0.98 E02 TempCNN 0.912 [0.848, 0.955] 0.845 [0.722, 0.922] +0.018 [−0.017, +0.053] 0.65 E03 U-TAE running E04 frozen GeoFMs (6 encoders) running

No difference counts so far: every CI of the paired differences includes 0. The Holm-adjusted p-values are provisional and will be recomputed when E03 and E04 join the family.

So far. The pixel classifiers reach macro-F1 0.89–0.91. The errors are mostly rainfed pixels taken for irrigated, in the wetter year 2024/25 and in Souss; TempCNN finds more of them than the tree ensembles. Rainfed parcels lie in three of the six zones, mostly in Doukkala, so the rainfed scores, and their wide confidence intervals, depend on few spatial blocks. Details: E01, E02.

docs.title: Pixel-wise experiment plan
docs.text: The experiments compare inputs, models and adaptation strategies for classifying the 10 m pixels of the surveyed parcels as irrigated or rainfed (D16, D19). The best model later produces the annual maps (Phase 5), where the cropland extent is decided. All experiments run for Morocco first; Utah follows with the same plan. Experiments run one at a time on the cluster; the results are copied to the Mac for the reports.

docs.title: 1. Common set-up (identical for every experiment)
docs.text:
Item Choice Samples the labelled pixels of 04_make_pixel_samples.py (Pixel samples): inner pixels of the surveyed parcels, at most 100 per parcel. Morocco: 473,675 pixels of 8,775 parcels (7,579 irrigated, 1,196 rainfed) in 2,015 tiles Classes 1 irrigated · 2 rainfed (no cropland mask, no not-cropland class; D19) Regions and years Morocco first: 2023/24 and 2024/25 pooled, each pixel with its own year (as in D2). Utah afterwards: train and test on 2023/24 (WRLU 2024); 2020/21 only for the temporal test (RQ3) Input imagery Sentinel-2 only (D14): 12 monthly composites of the agricultural year × 12 bands, from the same tile store for every model Validation PASTIS rotation over the 5 spatial folds (20 km blocks; Morocco about 1,500 irrigated and 240 rainfed parcels per fold): 3 folds train, the next fold validation (early stopping, hyperparameters), 1 fold test; 5 rounds, so every pixel is tested once Same test pixels every experiment is scored on the same out-of-fold pixels. Models that work on whole tiles (E03–E05) predict the tile and are read at the sampled pixels Class imbalance class weights inversely proportional to the training-pixel counts (Morocco: rainfed pixels ≈ 1 : 8 irrigated, so a rainfed pixel counts about 8 times more) Seeds neural models: 3 seeds (42, 1042, 2042), mean probability; classical models: seed 42

Metrics (all from the out-of-fold predictions):

  • Headline: macro-F1, the mean F1 of irrigated and rainfed, so the minority class (rainfed) counts as much as the majority.
  • Per-class F1, precision and recall (rainfed recall: how many rainfed pixels are found); overall accuracy; confusion matrix.
  • 95% confidence intervals by block bootstrap over the 20 km blocks; two inputs or models are compared by the paired difference on the same pixels; a difference counts when its CI excludes 0 and Holm-corrected p < 0.05 (evaluation protocol).
  • Results per region, per year (Morocco) and per zone.

docs.title: 2. Experiments
docs.text:
ID Question Input Model Compute Order E01 How well do the raw Sentinel-2 pixel time series separate irrigated from rainfed? (baseline) 12 months × 12 bands per pixel (144 values) + NDVI, NDWI per month random forest; histogram gradient boosting CPU 1 E02 Does a temporal neural network beat the classical baseline on the same pixels? same pixel time series TempCNN (Pelletier et al. 2019) GPU 2 E03 Does a spatio-temporal network trained from scratch on the whole tile beat the pixel models? 128 × 128 px tiles, 12 months U-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2021) GPU 3 E04 Do frozen geospatial foundation models with a light decoder beat the pixel models? (RQ1) 128 × 128 px tiles, 12 months frozen Prithvi-EO-2.0, Clay v1.5, TerraMind, AgriFM and the pixel time-series models Presto, TESSERA + UPerNet decoder (PANGAEA; Marsocci et al. 2024), L-TAE over time for the single-date image models GPU 4 E05 Does fine-tuning (LoRA or full) beat the frozen encoder and the same network trained from scratch, and how does this depend on the number of labelled parcels? (RQ2) 128 × 128 px tiles, 12 months; 10 / 25 / 50 / 100% of the training parcels Prithvi-EO-2.0 + L-TAE + UPerNet (as E04): frozen, LoRA, fully fine-tuned, from scratch GPU 5

Run order (Morocco): E01 first (it fixes the evaluation code and gives the reference numbers), then the other pixel model (E02), then the tile models (E03 before E04, because U-TAE tests the tile training pipeline without the large encoders), then E05. Jobs: 1 CPU + 24 GPU (E02 1, E03 1, E04 6, E05 16); the same set again for Utah afterwards.

docs.title: Details per experiment
docs.text:
E01 · Sentinel-2 pixel baseline. The pixel's 12 × 12 band values in reflectance × 10,000, plus NDVI and NDWI per month; months without a clear observation are filled by linear interpolation in time. Random forest (500 trees, class_weight = "balanced") and histogram gradient boosting (class-weighted samples), hyperparameters chosen on the validation fold. Permutation importance per month and band. This answers how far a per-pixel time series alone goes; random forests are the standard in operational irrigation mapping (Ketchum et al. 2020; Xie et al. 2021).

E02 · temporal neural network. The same 12-step input, normalised per band with training-fold statistics. TempCNN (three 1-D convolution layers over the months); trained with weighted cross-entropy and early stopping on the validation fold; 3 seeds. Tests whether learnt temporal features beat the random forest. (A pixel-wise L-TAE was also run; it is on hold and not reported.) All runs are compared on the comparison page.

E03 · U-TAE from scratch. The PASTIS segmentation baseline: U-Net encoder with L-TAE attention over the 12 months, trained on the same tiles with the same masked loss. Shows how much the pretrained encoders add over a spatio-temporal network of the same input.

E04 · frozen foundation models + decoder. The encoders see whole 128 px tiles (16 px patches for Prithvi and AgriFM's settings, 8 px for Clay), one month at a time or all months as the model allows; the patch features are combined over time with L-TAE and brought back to 10 m by a UPerNet decoder, trained with a masked loss on the labelled pixels of each tile (irrigated and rainfed; all other pixels ignored). Only the decoder and temporal head are trained. Same normalisations and band choices as in the archived embedding scripts (loaders in pixelwise_run/encoders.py) (D12, D15). The two pixel time-series models, Presto (Tseng et al. 2023) and TESSERA v2 (Feng et al. 2025, 2026), encode the 12-month series of every pixel of the tile into a 128-d vector; the 10 m feature map goes to the same UPerNet head (Foundation models).

E05 · Prithvi: frozen, LoRA, fine-tuned or from scratch. The E04 network with Prithvi, trained four ways: encoder frozen (E04), low-rank adapters (LoRA, rank 16, on the attention and MLP layers) trained on the frozen encoder, every encoder weight trained from the pretrained weights (encoder learning rate 10⁻⁵, head 10⁻⁴), or every weight trained from random weights. Each with 10, 25, 50 and 100% of the training-fold parcels (per class, nested draws; validation and test folds complete). Loss and F1 per epoch, score against the share of parcels, and paired tests per share (E05).

docs.title: 3. After the experiments
docs.text:
1. Temporal test (RQ3), Utah: the best models trained on 2023/24 and applied to 2020/21 on the test folds.
  2. Maps (Phase 5): the best model on wall-to-wall Sentinel-2 composites; the cropland extent is decided here (candidate masks such as the union of products or Dynamic World, compared on the omission of surveyed irrigated and rainfed parcels and on commission; D19); irrigated and rainfed area per region and year. Two independent approaches: the experiments above use the Earth Engine tiles; the STAC approach (s2_download/) downloads monthly composites (Earth Search, scene-classification cloud mask) for every cropland tile of the mask per 10.24 km block, and its models are trained, evaluated and mapped on those STAC tiles only (D18; status 20 Nov 2026: Utah 2023/24 17,278 of 18,472 tiles, the rest after a fix; Morocco on hold).
  3. Map accuracy: a stratified random sample over the map (including not-cropland), area-adjusted accuracy and area estimates (Olofsson et al. 2014); comparison with LGRIP30 and national statistics.

docs.title: 4. Optional ablations
docs.text:
• Sentinel-1 added to E01 / E02 (the tile store has it).
  • Fewer labels for the other models: 10 / 25 / 50% of the training parcels, as in E05 (Prithvi only).
  • A third class "not cropland" (weak labels from the cropland products), for the mapping phase: does a 3-class model remove false cropland better than a mask?
  • Stricter mask (≥ 2 votes) for the maps.

docs.title: 5. How an experiment runs
docs.text: Each experiment has a folder experiments/E0<N>_<name>/ with its run.py (settings at the top, no command-line arguments) and a page in this section; the shared code is listed on the overview. On the cluster every run is a Slurm job (jobs/step_cpu.sbatch or jobs/step_gpu.sbatch with SCRIPT=<run.py>); region, encoder and quick-test mode are passed as EXPERIMENT_REGION, EXPERIMENT_ENCODER and EXPERIMENT_QUICK_TEST. A run writes results/<region>/<run>/ (out-of-fold predictions per pixel, metrics with CI, per-group metrics, confusion matrix, settings); only results/ is copied to the Mac, where pixelwise_run/05_compare_experiments.py builds the comparison table and the paired tests, and the experiment page is filled in.

docs.title: Cropland extent and mask
docs.text:
The annual irrigated / rainfed maps are continuous (wall-to-wall): every 10 m pixel of a region's cropland gets a class, not only the surveyed parcels. This page describes the area those maps cover, the cropland mask, and the reference layers drawn for comparison. The code is in cropland_extent/; all outputs are in outputs/<region>/cropland_extent/.

Mapping phase only

The cropland mask belongs to the mapping phase (Phase 5). The labels, the pixel samples and the experiments E01–E05 do not use it: they classify the labelled pixels of the surveyed parcels, which are all cropland, as irrigated or rainfed (pixel samples). Only the wall-to-wall mapping tiles (s2_download/, pixelwise_run/06_build_cropland_tiles.py) read the mask. Which mask the maps use, and how land that is not cropland is handled, is decided later, for example by comparing the union of products described here with Dynamic World alone (D19).

Script What it does Output (in outputs/<region>/cropland_extent/) make_cropland_mask.py cropland mask per region and agricultural year from 4 cropland products (Earth Engine) cropland_mask/<season>/ download_esa_worldcover.py ESA WorldCover 2021, 10 m GeoTIFF + PNG map esa_worldcover/ download_lgrip30.py LGRIP30 irrigated / rainfed cropland, 30 m GeoTIFF + PNG map lgrip30/ download_dynamic_world.py annual Dynamic World 10 m layer per agricultural year (Earth Engine): most frequent class, mean crop probability, number of images; GeoTIFF on the project grid + PNG map dynamic_world/

All four use the same area: the region's mapping area in pixelwise_run/regions.py, i.e. Morocco without Western Sahara (FAO GAUL 2015, 414,905 km²) and the state of Utah (FAO GAUL 2024, 219,809 km²).

docs.title: 1. Why a mask from several products
docs.text:
A single cropland product misses cropland: small fields, fallow land, orchards, recent expansion. On the parcels of the first test (3,498 surveyed irrigated parcels in Morocco), single products covered 78% (WorldCover) to 99% (GCEP30) of them; their union covered 100%. A pixel is therefore cropland if at least one of the products calls it cropland. Combining products to reduce omission is established practice: Meier et al. (2018) restricted irrigation mapping to cropland of two land-cover products combined, LANID (Xie et al. 2021) took the cultivated area of any year, and LGRIP30 added cropland that its own extent map missed (Teluguntla et al. 2023).

The price of the union is extra non-cropland inside the mask. How the maps handle it is open and is decided in the mapping phase: a stricter mask (more votes, or a single product such as Dynamic World), or an extra "not cropland" class learnt by the classifier, as IrrMapper did instead of an external mask (Ketchum et al. 2020). The mask is applied to the map output; the model never sees masked inputs.

The mask uses no field labels (neither the Moroccan survey nor WRLU), so its quality is the same in labelled and unlabelled areas. The training data do not depend on the mask: no labelled parcel is checked against it or dropped.

docs.title: 2. Products
docs.text:
The year of a product is the calendar year in which the agricultural year ends, clipped to the years the product has (2023/24 → 2024).

Product Earth Engine asset Resolution · year(s) Cropland = Source ESA WorldCover v200 ESA/WorldCover/v200 10 m · 2021 class 40 Zanaga et al. 2022, doi:10.5281/zenodo.7254221 · GEE catalogue Esri / Impact Observatory LULC projects/sat-io/open-datasets/landcover/ESRI_Global-LULC_10m_TS 10 m · annual 2017–2025 class 5 (crops) Karra et al. 2021 (IGARSS) · community catalogue GCEP30 (GFSAD) projects/sat-io/open-datasets/GFSAD/GCEP30 30 m · 2015 value 2 Thenkabail et al. 2021, USGS PP 1868 · community catalogue GLAD global cropland users/potapovpeter/Global_cropland_2019 30 m · 2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019 value 1 Potapov et al. 2022, doi:10.1038/s43016-021-00429-z · GLAD
  • GCEP30 is stored as continental tiles that overlap and disagree in Morocco (the Europe / Middle East tile has almost no cropland there). The flags are combined with the maximum over the tiles, not with a mosaic.
  • Tree crops: WorldCover maps orchards as tree cover and GLAD excludes perennial woody crops, so orchards depend on the Esri and GCEP30 layers.
  • Not used in the union (kept in the script as options with fixed bit numbers): Dynamic World (too slow per block and Earth Engine memory errors; an annual Dynamic World layer is downloaded separately by download_dynamic_world.py, §7), ESA WorldCereal 2021 temporary crops, LGRIP30 (same extent as GCEP30 in the test), GLC_FCS30D, and the USDA Cropland Data Layer for Utah.
  • Always removed: WorldCover 2021 built-up (50), snow and ice (70) and permanent water (80); these pixels are never mapped.

docs.title: 3. How the mask is made
docs.text:
1. Blocks on the tile grid. Earth Engine returns at most 48 MB per request, and Morocco at 10 m has about 10 billion pixels. The mapping area is cut into blocks of 1024 × 1024 px (10.24 km) on the same grid as the tiles of 03_build_tiles.py (x = ix × 1280 m), so every block holds whole 128 px tiles. Morocco has 4,199 blocks, Utah 2,213; 8 blocks are downloaded in parallel at about 0.5 s per block; finished blocks are skipped on a re-run.
  2. One request per block returns one bit per product and the exclusion flag; votes and the mask are computed locally.
  3. One raster per agricultural year. cropland_mask.vrt joins all blocks into one seamless layer.
  4. Tile table. tiles_cropland.parquet lists every 128 px tile with its number of cropland pixels: the input of the wall-to-wall tiles (s2_download/; earlier route pixelwise_run/06_build_cropland_tiles.py).

Bands of the mask (uint16, NODATA 65535 outside the mapping area):

Band Content cropland the mask: 1 if ≥ MIN_VOTES products (1 = union) call the pixel cropland and it is not excluded votes number of products that call the pixel cropland (0–4) products bit flags, one bit per product (WorldCover 0, Esri 1, GCEP30 4, GLAD 6) excluded 1 = WorldCover built-up, snow / ice or water

The vote count and the flags allow a stricter mask (for example ≥ 2 votes) or another product set later without a new download.

docs.title: 4. Results, 2023/24
docs.text:
Morocco Utah Mapping area 414,906 km² 219,809 km² Cropland (union, ≥ 1 vote) 103,068 km² (24.8%) 9,979 km² (4.5%) Cropland with ≥ 2 votes 73,886 km² 6,000 km² Removed as built-up / snow / water 3,087 km² 6,382 km² 128 px tiles with cropland 132,616 24,861

Cropland of each product, and the area that only this product calls cropland (what it adds to the union):

Product Morocco: cropland Morocco: only this product Utah: cropland Utah: only this product WorldCover 2021 64,122 km² (62% of the union) 6,474 km² 3,427 km² (34%) 110 km² Esri LULC 2024 50,876 km² (49%) 2,950 km² 5,977 km² (60%) 1,251 km² GCEP30 2015 83,937 km² (81%) 16,233 km² 7,742 km² (78%) 2,121 km² GLAD 2019 62,998 km² (61%) 3,526 km² 5,650 km² (57%) 498 km²

GCEP30 is the most generous product and adds most of the area seen by one product only, mostly at the margins of the cropland belts (right-hand panels below). Most of the union's false cropland is expected there; the choice of mask in the mapping phase and the map accuracy assessment address it.

Left: share of cropland per 1.28 km tile. Right: share of the mask's pixels that only one product calls cropland.

docs.title: 5. Extent of the wall-to-wall tiles
docs.text:
Mapping the whole cropland means imagery for every tile that contains cropland: 132,616 tiles in Morocco (about 370 GB of monthly Sentinel-2 composites per year) and 24,861 in Utah (about 69 GB), against 2,183 and 2,720 tiles around the labelled parcels. Morocco's cropland forms one continuous belt from Tangier to Agadir (a quarter of the country), and scattered fields pull in whole 1.64 km² tiles.

STAC download. The wall-to-wall tiles are downloaded with s2_download/ from the public Earth Search STAC catalogue (collection sentinel-2-c1-l2a, cloud mask from the scene classification layer SCL, monthly median composites; details in s2_download/README.md). It keeps the tiles with at least 1% cropland: 112,536 tiles in Morocco and 18,472 in Utah for 2023/24 (Morocco 2024/25: 113,319). The tiles follow the grid and tile_id of the mask and serve training, experiments and maps of the STAC-based approach.

Region Year Tiles (≥ 1% cropland) Status Utah 2023/24 18,472 🔄 17,278 downloaded; the rest to be rerun after a bug fix Morocco 2023/24 112,536 on hold

The earlier Earth Engine route for the same tiles (pixelwise_run/06_build_cropland_tiles.py) is still in the repository. The experiments E01–E05 use the Earth Engine tiles around the labelled parcels (03_build_tiles.py).

docs.title: 6. Check against the labelled parcels
docs.text: The label scripts (pixelwise_run/01_prepare_labels_*.py) no longer read the mask, and the pixel samples contain the surveyed parcels only, whether or not they lie inside the mask. The check of a candidate mask against the surveyed parcels is part of the mask choice in the mapping phase: the omission of surveyed irrigated and of surveyed rainfed parcels (cropland the mask misses) and the commission (land in the mask that is not cropland), for the union of products, for Dynamic World alone and for stricter variants (Phase 5).

docs.title: 7. Reference layers
docs.text:
ESA WorldCover and LGRIP30 are drawn as reference maps for the documentation and for comparing the final maps; the mask reads its products directly in Earth Engine. download_dynamic_world.py builds an annual Dynamic World layer per agricultural year (Brown et al. 2022): the most frequent class of the year (label), the mean probability of the class "crops" in percent (crops) and the number of Dynamic World images (n_obs), on the 10 m grid of the tiles and the mask. It is a candidate for the mask of the maps (by class, or by a threshold on the crop probability); no model or dataset script uses it. Colours: WorldCover's official palette; LGRIP30 water #0050cb, non-cropland #d58855, irrigated #c2d30c, rainfed #379a4b. The PNG maps are reduced to 2,500 px for display (mode resampling) from the original 10 m and 30 m GeoTIFFs.

Morocco Utah ESA WorldCover 2021 LGRIP30 (nominal 2015)

LGRIP30 calls 11.7% of Morocco irrigated and 8.7% rainfed, including large parts of the rainfed Gharb and Chaouia plains; it is a reference layer, not ground truth.

docs.title: Morocco training data
docs.text:
This page describes the construction of the machine-learning-ready dataset for Morocco: labelled parcels, spatial train / validation / test folds, a common store of monthly Sentinel-1/2 imagery with label rasters, and the labelled pixels of the surveyed parcels (two classes: irrigated, rainfed) from which every pixel-wise experiment starts (D16). The models use the Sentinel-2 bands only (D14).

Archived: parcel-wise set-up

Parts of this page (the model views A–C of section 7 and their use in section 9) describe the archived parcel-wise set-up. They are kept for reference and marked as archived; see the Archive and Parcel-wise classification.

Contents

  1. Overview
  2. Design principles
  3. Source data
  4. Script 01 — labels

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TD subgraph IN["Inputs"] FS["Field survey<br/>~10,000 parcels<br/>Dec 2023 – Jan 2025"] GEE["Google Earth Engine<br/>Sentinel-2 L2A · Cloud Score+<br/>Sentinel-1 GRD"] end FS --> S01["<b>01_prepare_labels_Morocco.py</b><br/>clean geometry · label · cropland only<br/>agricultural year"] S01 -->|"parcels_labelled.geojson<br/>8,781 parcels"| S02["<b>02_make_spatial_folds.py</b><br/>20 km blocks → 5 balanced folds"] S02 -->|"parcels_folds.geojson<br/>+ block_id, fold"| SPLIT[["Split by agricultural year<br/>(ag_season from survey date)"]] SPLIT -->|"2023/24 · 6,887 parcels<br/>imagery Sep 2023 – Aug 2024"| S03["<b>03_build_tiles.py</b><br/>run per agricultural year:<br/>128 × 128 px tiles · 12 months × 19 bands<br/>label / parcel-ID / edge rasters"] SPLIT -->|"2024/25 · 1,894 parcels<br/>imagery Sep 2024 – Aug 2025"| S03 GEE --> S03 S03 -->|"tiles/ · parcels.csv · tiles.parquet"| S04["<b>04_make_pixel_samples.py</b><br/>labelled parcel pixels: irrigated · rainfed<br/>12 months, fold, position"] S04 --> PX["Pixel models<br/>(E01, E02)"] S03 --> VD["Full tiles<br/>(tile models E03–E05)"] S03 -.->|"archived"| S04A["parcelwise_run/04_make_views.py<br/>views A–C (parcel-wise)"] Step Script What comes out 1 01_prepare_labels_Morocco.py 8,781 labelled cropland parcels (7,585 irrigated, 1,196 rainfed) 2 02_make_spatial_folds.py a fold (0–4) per parcel, from 91 spatial blocks of 20 km 3 03_build_tiles.py the tile store: monthly images + label rasters + QA 4 04_make_pixel_samples.py labelled pixels of the surveyed parcels (irrigated, rainfed) per agricultural year: 367,882 (2023/24) and 105,793 (2024/25) 4 (archived) parcelwise_run/04_make_views.py parcel-wise model views A–C

Steps 1–2 complete within minutes. Step 3 requires several hours and resumes from the last completed tile when restarted. Step 4 runs locally.

docs.title: 2. Design principles
docs.text:
Principle How it is achieved One set of pixels for every model All imagery is downloaded once into one tile store. Every model input is cut from it locally, so differences between models cannot come from different compositing, masks or download windows. No duplicated downloads Fixed, non-overlapping 1.28 km tiles in one projection. Neighbouring parcels share tiles instead of each getting its own overlapping chip. Imagery matched to the label date Each parcel gets the 12 months of the agricultural year (1 Sep – 31 Aug) in which it was surveyed. The same place in another year is a different tile. Honest validation Folds are made of whole 20 km blocks, so a test parcel never has its next-door neighbour in training (section 5). Uncertain pixels kept, not dropped Label 0 = ignore (unlabelled or overlapping parcels), plus a separate edge flag for mixed boundary pixels. Users decide how to treat them. Documented quality Clear-observation counts per pixel and month, scene IDs per tile and month, QA per tile, overlap list, patch-purity scores. Patch-aware chips (archived parcel-wise views) Chips for patch-based models were shifted so the parcel centroid sits at the centre of one model patch (section 7).

The layout follows existing ML-ready crop datasets. PASTIS (Garnot & Landrieu 2021) and Sen4AgriNet (Sykas et al. 2022) use fixed tiles with dense label and parcel-ID rasters. Fields of The World (Kerner et al. 2025) keeps an "unlabelled" ignore class. The ClarkCGA / Prithvi crop chips report QA counts per chip.
