docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
Step Script What comes out 1 01_prepare_labels_Utah.py 12,015 labelled crop fields in 550 sampled cells: WRLU 2024 (5,000 irrigated, 1,013 rainfed) and WRLU 2021 (4,987 irrigated, 1,015 rainfed); plus all 245,648 labelled crop fields of both years before sampling 2 02_make_spatial_folds.py (REGION = "utah") a fold (0–4) per field, from 183 spatial blocks of 20 km 3 03_build_tiles.py (REGION = "utah") tile plan: 5,436 tiles (2,720 for 2023/24, 2,716 for 2020/21); label rasters written 4 04_make_pixel_samples.py (REGION = "utah") labelled pixels of the crop fields (irrigated, rainfed) per year (04_pixel_samples/<season>/): 2023/24 to be rebuilt with the two-class script

All outputs are in outputs/utah/dataset/ (01_labels/, 02_folds/, 03_tiles_128px/agyear/, 04_pixel_samples/), with the same file names and columns as outputs/morocco/dataset/.

docs.title: 2. Study design
docs.text:
• Utah is an independent second study area. There is no Morocco → Utah transfer: each region is trained and tested on its own data, with the same pipeline, foundation models, classifiers and evaluation, and the results are reported side by side. This tests whether the conclusions from Morocco hold in a second region with other crops, climate and labels.
  • Two questions in Utah:
    1. how well the models separate irrigated and rainfed pixels (spatial cross-validation, as in Morocco);
    2. temporal transferability: whether a model trained on one year still works in another year (section 10).
  • Training year: WRLU 2024 (agricultural year 2023/24). Temporal test year: WRLU 2021 (2020/21).

docs.title: 3. Why Utah
docs.text:
The candidates were compared in D10 (Tunisia, eastern Washington, Utah, the IrrMap states):

  • An explicit rainfed class. The WRLU metadata defines IRR_Method = "Dry Crop" as a field with no irrigation, watered by natural processes (rain). IrrMap labels only the irrigation method (no rainfed class), and Colorado (CRDSS) and most layers of the USGS verified irrigated lands are irrigated-only.
  • Enough rainfed fields: 13,000–17,000 rainfed crop fields every year (figure below). Tunisia has 10 rainfed GMIA-NEXT points.
  • Every year from 2017 to 2025, mapped by one agency with one method, so the same pipeline also gives a temporal test.

WRLU crop fields (grain/seeds, hay/turf, field crops) per year and class, before sampling.

docs.title: 4. Source data
docs.text: Data Use Details Water-Related Land Use (WRLU), Utah Division of Water Resources labels one polygon layer per year, 2017–2025; all agricultural fields of Utah and of the parts of its river basins in Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, Nevada and Arizona; crop (Descriptio, CropGroup), irrigation method (IRR_Method), basin, county, state. In data/Utah_field_data/ FAO GAUL 2024 (level 1) maps state outlines (data/admin_boundaries/) Sentinel-2 L2A, Cloud Score+, Sentinel-1 GRD imagery as for Morocco (Google Earth Engine); the models use Sentinel-2 only (D14) Sentinel-2 L2A (Earth Search STAC, sentinel-2-c1-l2a) wall-to-wall imagery s2_download/, every tile with ≥ 1% cropland

docs.title: 5. Which years, and how the labels change between years
docs.text:
Agricultural year. WRLU year Y describes the crops of the growing season Y. The dataset uses the US water year, 1 October (Y−1) to 30 September (Y), written as for Morocco: WRLU 2024 → 2023/24, WRLU 2021 → 2020/21. It covers winter wheat from its autumn sowing to the July harvest, the whole irrigation season (mid-April to mid-October) and June–September, when irrigated and dry crops differ most. A calendar year would start in snow and cut off the autumn sowing. As in Morocco, every field gets the 12 monthly composites of its own year.

How much changes between years. All labelled crop fields of each year (the whole of WRLU, not only the sample) were compared with WRLU 2024. A field counts as the same field when its outline overlaps a 2024 outline with an intersection over union above 0.8 (outputs/utah/dataset/01_labels/year_change_vs_2024.csv):

WRLU year Labelled crop fields Same outline as in 2024 Crop changed Irrigation method changed Class changed (irrigated ↔ rainfed) 2024 122,624 (15,276 rainfed) – – – – 2025 123,722 121,811 (98.5%) 6.3% 17.4%¹ 28 (0.02%) 2023 121,029 116,492 (96.3%) 27.1% 0.1% 17 (0.01%) 2021 123,024 110,821 (90.1%) 35.7% 0.7% 83 (0.07%) 2019 121,063 100,491 (83.0%) 38.0% 2.7% 1,352 (1.35%) 2017 117,901 92,054 (78.1%) 40.6% 3.0% 1,307 (1.42%)

¹ Mostly a change of coding: in 2025 WRLU split Sprinkler into Sprinkler, Pivot and Wheel (wheel line).

  • Field outlines change slowly (78–98% unchanged).
  • Crops change a lot through rotation (27–41% after 1–7 years).
  • Irrigated vs rainfed hardly ever changes (0.01–0.07% since 2021). In Utah, irrigation depends on a water right and on canals, pivots and wells tied to the land; part of the stability may also come from labels carried over between map updates, which the data cannot separate.

Choice of years:

  • WRLU 2024 = training year: recent, actively updated (27% of the crops changed from 2023), and it overlaps the Moroccan survey years.
  • WRLU 2021 = temporal test year: three years earlier; 36% of the crops differ from 2024 while the labels stay consistent (83 class changes in 123,024 fields), so the test isolates the change of year (crops, weather, timing). 2021 was a drought year in Utah (drought emergency declared in March 2021), a realistic year-to-year shift that is reported as context. It still has both Sentinel-1 satellites (Sentinel-1B failed in December 2021).
  • Not 2025: 94% of its crops repeat 2024, so it looks largely carried over and is no independent test.
  • Not 2019 (for now): the jump from 83 class changes (2021) to 1,352 (2019) is sudden and may come from a revision of the mapping rather than from real change; it would need checking first.
  • Not all years: the labels are near-copies, so more years add volume but little information, at about 10 GB of tiles per year.

docs.title: 6. Script 01 — labels
docs.text:
1. Source inspection for every year in FILES: fields and area per crop group and irrigation method (source_counts.csv, source_years.png).
  2. Read the years in YEARS (agricultural fields only) and clean the geometry as for Morocco: repair invalid polygons, drop empty and duplicate geometries.

  3. Label:

    IRR_Method Label Flood, Sprinkler, Drip; from 2025 also Pivot and Wheel 1 · irrigated Dry Crop 2 · rainfed Sub-irrigated (natural high water table) dropped: neither class

  4. Crop fields only (CROP_GROUPS): grain/seeds, hay/turf and field crops. Fallow/idle land and pasture are dropped (no crop to observe, or grazing land rather than cropland). Garden, orchard and small fruit are dropped too: they are small groups, and orchards are almost all irrigated in Utah (19 "Dry Crop" orchards in 2023), so they would only add an easy irrigated class.

  5. All labelled crop fields before sampling (EXPORT_ALL_FIELDS = True): every labelled crop field of YEARS goes to all_crop_fields.gpkg (for QGIS) with a column sampled that marks the fields of the sampled cells, plus summary tables and figures, so the sample can be compared with the whole population:

    WRLU year Irrigated Rainfed In the sample 2024 107,348 15,276 5,000 irrigated (4.7%), 1,013 rainfed (6.6%) 2021 107,035 15,989 4,987 irrigated (4.7%), 1,015 rainfed (6.3%)

  6. Attributes with the Morocco names: parcel_id (UT<year>_<feature id>), ag_season, label, class_name, crop, zone (= river basin), area_ha, nn_dist_m (nearest field of the same year). Utah extras: year, state, county, crop_group, irr_method, cell_id. WRLU has no survey date, so date is empty.

How many fields are dropped on the way (WRLU 2024): 283,781 polygons in the file → 190,269 agricultural (urban, water, wetland and other land removed) → 122,624 labelled crop fields (fallow, pasture, sub-irrigated, orchard, garden and small fruit removed) → 6,013 in the sampled cells.

All labelled crop fields of WRLU 2024 and 2021 before sampling.

Main crops per class, all labelled crop fields of both years. Alfalfa is the main crop of both classes.

docs.title: 7. Script 01 — sampling of cells
docs.text:
Why a sample and not all fields. All labelled crop fields would be about 122,000 fields per year: roughly 20,000 tiles (~75 GB) per year and 15–20 times the model run time of Morocco, for little extra independent information. The statistics are limited by the rainfed class and by the number of spatial blocks, not by the number of fields: fields in the same block are strongly alike (89% of field pairs closer than 1 km share their class), and the block bootstrap counts blocks. The sample also keeps the Utah dataset close to the size of the Moroccan one (8,781 parcels), so model differences are not a matter of data volume.

Three nested units:

Unit Size Role Field median 2.5 ha one sample with its label Cell 1.28 × 1.28 km = one 128-px tile of script 03 the sampling unit: a cell is sampled with all its fields, or not at all Block 20 × 20 km (~240 cells) the fold unit of script 02; also used to spread the sample

Both grids start at the origin of UTM 12N: cell = (⌊x / 1,280 m⌋, ⌊y / 1,280 m⌋), block = (⌊x / 20,000 m⌋, ⌊y / 20,000 m⌋). A field belongs to the cell and to the block that contain its centroid.

Algorithm (sample_cells: stratified random sampling with a cap per block):

  1. Cells with at least one labelled crop field in any of YEARS (both years pooled): 12,424 cells.
  2. Two strata: "with rainfed" = at least one rainfed field in either year; "irrigated only" = the rest.
  3. Random order within each stratum (fixed seed SEED = 42, so every run gives the same cells).
  4. Cap: going down the shuffled list, a cell is skipped once its 20 km block already has MAX_CELLS_PER_BLOCK (6) cells of that stratum. Without the cap the densest valleys (Cache Valley, Bear River) would take most of the sample.
  5. The first N_RAINFED_CELLS (400) and N_IRRIGATED_CELLS (150) cells are kept: 550 cells in 176 blocks.
  6. The same cells are used for every year in YEARS; every labelled crop field inside a sampled cell is kept.

What is labelled inside a sampled tile:

In the tile Label raster crop fields (grain, hay, field crops), irrigated or Dry Crop, whose centroid lies in the cell 1 irrigated / 2 rainfed fallow, pasture, orchards, sub-irrigated fields 0 = ignore roads, towns, natural land 0 = ignore a field centred in a neighbouring, not sampled cell that reaches into the tile 0 = ignore

A labelled field is always complete: when its outline crosses into the next tile, that tile is built as well ("outline" tile). Within a 20 km block at most 12 cells (6 + 6) are sampled, i.e. at most ~5% of its area is labelled. Labels are therefore dense within a sampled cell and sparse within a block, as in Morocco, where the survey did not label every field either.

Result:

Agricultural year Irrigated Rainfed Rainfed share 2020/21 (WRLU 2021, test year) 4,987 1,015 16.9% 2023/24 (WRLU 2024, training year) 5,000 1,013 16.8% Total 9,987 2,028 16.9%

Rainfed fields are over-represented on purpose (16.9% of the sample against 12.5–13% of all fields), which makes the rainfed F1 more reliable. Median field size is 2.5 ha in both classes, three times the Moroccan median (0.83 ha). By state: 8,234 + 1,057 fields in Utah, 1,707 + 849 in Idaho (Bear River basin), the rest in Colorado and Wyoming (irrigated + rainfed). 1,171 of the 2,028 rainfed fields (58%) are in the Bear River basin.

Cells of 1.28 km with crop fields in WRLU 2024 or 2021 (grey) and the sampled cells: with a rainfed field in either year (red), irrigated only (blue). The same cells are used for both years.

Sampled reference fields, WRLU 2024 and 2021.

Main crops per class in the sample. Rainfed fields are mostly dryland alfalfa, winter wheat and grass hay.

Larger samples are a change of N_RAINFED_CELLS / N_IRRIGATED_CELLS and a re-run of 01–03:

Option Cells Fields per year (approx.) Cost relative to now now 400 + 150 ~6,000 1× double 800 + 300 ~12,000 ~2× all cells with rainfed + matching irrigated-only ~4,800 + 1,500 ~60,000 ~10× all fields (SAMPLE = False) ~12,400 ~122,000 ~20×

Outputs (outputs/utah/dataset/01_labels/): parcels_labelled.geojson (the sample), source_counts.csv, summary.csv, summary_by_zone.csv, sampled_cells.csv, year_change_vs_2024.csv; before sampling: all_crop_fields.gpkg, all_fields_summary.csv, all_fields_by_zone.csv, all_fields_*.png; figures.

docs.title: 8. Script 02 — spatial folds
docs.text:
The same script as for Morocco (REGION = "utah"). The class-similarity curve uses only pairs of fields of the same agricultural year: the same field in two years is not two independent samples.

Distance between fields ≤ 0.25 km 1 km 3 km 10 km 15 km 20 km random placement Pairs with the same class 92.1% 89.2% 80.2% 80.2% 70.5% 70.7% 71.9%

Class similarity reaches the random-placement level at about 15 km, so the 20 km block of Morocco is kept.

Split (average over the 5 rounds) Rainfed in smallest fold Test with train ≤ 250 m Test with train ≤ 1 km random 405 94.3% 99.4% blocks 5 km 405 6.5% 27.7% blocks 20 km 405 2.2% 9.8% blocks 50 km 336 0.3% 2.1%

Folds: 183 blocks, about 2,000 irrigated and 405 rainfed fields per fold. A field belongs to the block of its centroid, so the same place falls in the same block, and therefore in the same fold, in every year: a model is never trained on a place it is tested on, in either year. The greedy assignment places the blocks with the most rainfed fields first; the many small blocks with few fields come last, so one fold (here fold 0, 59 blocks) collects more, smaller blocks than the others (30–33). Morocco shows the same pattern (fold 2: 42 of 91 blocks).

Fields coloured by fold (left) and class counts per fold (right).

The 20 km blocks coloured by fold, with enlargements of the two densest areas: A on the Utah–Idaho border (Cache Valley, Bear River), B in central Utah. Whole blocks go to one fold.

docs.title: 9. Script 03 — tile store
docs.text:
The same script as for Morocco (REGION = "utah"). Grid, bands, cloud mask and file formats are unchanged (Morocco, section 6). Two settings come from regions.py: the projection (UTM 12N, EPSG:32612) and the first month (October, so m01 = October).

One tile per place and year. The tile name starts with the agricultural year, so the same place gets one tile per year, on the same pixel grid:

Training year (WRLU 2024) Test year (WRLU 2021) tile 2023-24_184_3383 2020-21_184_3383 image _img.tif Sentinel-1/2, Oct 2023 – Sep 2024 Sentinel-1/2, Oct 2020 – Sep 2021 label _lab.tif the 2024 fields and labels the 2021 fields and labels field in parcels.csv own parcel_id / parcel_idx own parcel_id / parcel_idx fold e.g. fold 3 the same fold 3

The tiles store Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 bands, but every model uses the Sentinel-2 bands only (D14).

parcels.csv holds both years (6,013 fields of 2023/24 and 6,002 of 2020/21); their numbers never change when another year is downloaded.

Tile plan (DOWNLOAD = False): 12,015 fields; 6 smaller than one pixel centre; 280 with no pixel left after the 10 m inner buffer; no overlapping fields. 5,436 tiles (2,720 for 2023/24, 2,716 for 2020/21; 1,042 home tiles), about 10 GB of images per year. 120 tiles hold fields of two folds: a 20 km block is 15.6 cells wide, so some cells straddle a block border (pixel samples take the fold of their parcel; tile models need the loss mask, as in Morocco).

docs.title: 10. Temporal test design
docs.text:
Because the training year and the test year use the same cells, the test fold holds the same fields in both years. Per round of the 5-fold rotation:

Score Train Test Measures A · same year 2024, training folds 2024, test fold spatial accuracy, as in Morocco B · new year, new places 2024, training folds 2021, test fold temporal transferability (main result) C · new year, seen places 2024, training folds 2021, training-fold fields change of imagery only (upper bound: places seen in training)
  • B − A is the cost of the change of year, measured on identical fields (a paired comparison, so the block bootstrap gives a narrow interval).
  • Within B, the fields whose crop changed between the two years show where a new year matters most.
  • The test asks whether a model recognises irrigation in a different year with other crops and weather. It cannot test the detection of changes in irrigation (83 class changes in the whole of WRLU).
  • The experiments read their years from SEASONS in pixelwise_run/pixel_common.py (Utah: 2023/24 only); the 2021 test needs the 2020/21 tile images and pixel samples first.

docs.title: 11. Differences from Morocco
docs.text: Morocco Utah Labels field survey, Dec 2023 – Jan 2025 agency land-use map (WRLU), mostly image interpretation; 1,987 fields field-checked in 2025 Rainfed definition "rainfed" in the survey IRR_Method = "Dry Crop" Crops seasonal crops and trees grain, hay and field crops (no orchards) Selection all surveyed parcels 550 sampled 1.28 km cells, all fields inside Years 2023/24 and 2024/25, pooled 2023/24 (training) and 2020/21 (temporal test), kept apart Agricultural year 1 Sep – 31 Aug 1 Oct – 30 Sep (water year) Projection UTM 29N UTM 12N zone irrigation district river basin Median field size 0.83 ha 2.5 ha Rainfed share 13.6% 16.9%

docs.title: 12. Running, one year at a time
docs.text:
conda activate condaml
python pixelwise_run/01_prepare_labels_Utah.py     # ~1 min; YEARS = [2024, 2021]
# in 02, 03 and 04 set REGION = "utah" at the top, then:
python pixelwise_run/02_make_spatial_folds.py      # seconds
python pixelwise_run/03_build_tiles.py             # SEASONS = ["2023/24"]; first N_TEST_TILES = 20; Earth Engine, resumable
python pixelwise_run/04_make_pixel_samples.py      # SEASONS per region in the script -> 04_pixel_samples/<season>/

Run everything in the condaml environment: another GDAL / GEOS version once gave one field more.

Step Runs for Why 01 labels, 02 folds all years in YEARS at once (local, ~1 min) sampled cells, parcel numbers and folds are fixed once, the same for every year 03 plan + label rasters all years (local, seconds) the parcel numbers in the label rasters never change 03 Earth Engine download only the years in SEASONS 2024 first (["2023/24"]), 2021 later (["2020/21"]); finished tiles are skipped 04 pixel samples only the years in SEASONS (each needs its tiles) each year in its own folder: 04_pixel_samples/2023-24/, 04_pixel_samples/2020-21/

Archived: parcel-wise set-up

The archived parcel-wise pipeline ran parcelwise_run/04_make_views.py (views A–C, views_2023-24/) and parcelwise_run/05_inspect_dataset.py at this step; see the Archive.

Running 01 with one year only and adding the other year later would redraw the cells and rebalance the folds, and the two years would no longer be paired.

Region settings (pixelwise_run/regions.py): crs_epsg = 32612, start_month = 10, block_km = 20, map boundaries. Utah settings in 01_prepare_labels_Utah.py: YEARS, CROP_GROUPS, EXCLUDE_CROPS, IRRIGATED_METHODS, RAINFED_METHODS, STATES, EXPORT_ALL_FIELDS, SAMPLE, CELL_M, N_RAINFED_CELLS, N_IRRIGATED_CELLS, MAX_CELLS_PER_BLOCK, SEED.

docs.title: 13. Known limitations
docs.text:
• Labels are not a field survey. WRLU is mapped mainly from imagery with field checks on part of the area, and lists the Cropland Data Layer among its inputs. Its errors are not known per field.
  • Labels barely change between years (section 5): the temporal test measures robustness to a new year, not change detection, and it must hold out space (score B).
  • Unequal inclusion probabilities. Rainfed areas are favoured, and cells in crowded blocks are less likely to be sampled. This is fine for comparing models (all see the same fields), but the scores are not unbiased accuracy estimates for all Utah fields; that would need sampling weights. The same holds for Morocco, whose survey is not a probability sample either.
  • Dryland alfalfa is the largest rainfed crop (1,122 of 2,028). It is perennial and green in spring, unlike the Moroccan rainfed cereals. EXCLUDE_CROPS = ["Alfalfa"] gives a sensitivity run.
  • Class and place: 58% of the rainfed fields lie in the Bear River basin (northern Utah and south-east Idaho), so results are also reported per basin, as per zone in Morocco.
  • Snow: December–February composites in northern Utah often show snow (Cloud Score+ does not mask snow); both classes are affected alike.
  • Sentinel-1: 2021 has both Sentinel-1 satellites, 2024 only Sentinel-1A, so about twice as many Sentinel-1 scenes per month in the test year.
  • No cropland mask in the labels: every WRLU field is cropland, so no mask check is made; the cropland mask serves the mapping phase only (Cropland extent and mask).

docs.title: Evaluation protocol
docs.text:
This protocol defines the rules common to all pixel-wise experiments (E01–E05) and makes their results comparable across inputs, models and experiments. Any deviation is stated on the experiment's page. The protocol of the earlier parcel-wise benchmark is kept in the archive.

Contents: 1 Task · 2 Splits · 3 Models · 4 Fairness rules · 5 Metrics · 6 Reading a result · 7 Reporting · References

docs.title: 1. Task and unit
docs.text:
Every labelled 10 m pixel of the surveyed parcels is classified into one of two classes: 1 irrigated or 2 rainfed (D16, D19). All surveyed parcels are cropland, so the experiments measure the irrigated / rainfed decision alone; no cropland mask is used, and the handling of land that is not cropland is left to the mapping phase (Phase 5). The labelled pixels are the inner pixels of the surveyed parcels, at most 100 per parcel (pixel samples). Every model is scored on the same labelled pixels.

All experiments run in Morocco first: 2023/24 and 2024/25 pooled, each pixel with its own year (473,675 pixels of 8,775 parcels, 7,579 irrigated and 1,196 rainfed, in 2,015 tiles). Utah (2023/24) follows later with the same plan and is analysed separately.

docs.title: 2. Spatial splits
docs.text:
Parcels are grouped into 20 km blocks, and the blocks into 5 folds with a similar class balance; a block is never split, and every labelled pixel takes the fold of its parcel's block. Fold assignment: Morocco dataset §5.

PASTIS rotation (Garnot & Landrieu 2021). Five rounds; in each, 3 folds train, the next fold is the validation fold, one fold is the test fold:

Round Train Validation (early stopping, settings) Test 1 2, 3, 4 1 0 2 3, 4, 0 2 1 3 4, 0, 1 3 2 4 0, 1, 2 4 3 5 1, 2, 3 0 4

The test fold is never used for any choice. After 5 rounds every labelled pixel has one out-of-fold prediction from a model that never saw its block. Models that work on whole 128 px tiles (E03–E05) predict the test tiles and are read at their labelled pixels; a tile with pixels of several folds contributes only its training-fold labels to the loss.

Why a rotation rather than one fixed split. (i) Every pixel is tested once, so the rainfed scores rest on all rainfed parcels instead of those of a single test fold. (ii) Five test areas show how strongly accuracy depends on the region. (iii) Settings are never chosen on the test fold, so the reported accuracy is not inflated by tuning (Varma & Simon 2006). Spatially separated folds follow Roberts et al. (2017) and Ploton et al. (2020): random splits of autocorrelated pixels overstate accuracy (Kattenborn et al. 2022).

docs.title: 3. Models and inputs
docs.text:
All inputs come from the same tile store: 12 monthly Sentinel-2 composites of the agricultural year, Sentinel-2 only (D14).

Experiment Input Models E01 pixel time series, 12 months × 12 bands (+ NDVI, NDWI) random forest, histogram gradient boosting E02 same pixel time series TempCNN (the pixel L-TAE is on hold) E03 128 × 128 px tiles U-TAE from scratch E04 128 × 128 px tiles six frozen foundation models (Prithvi, Clay, TerraMind, AgriFM, Presto, TESSERA) + L-TAE + feature pyramid + UPerNet (Foundation models) E05 128 × 128 px tiles, 10, 25, 50 or 100% of the training parcels Prithvi frozen, LoRA, fully fine-tuned, from scratch (four strategies)

Neural models: class-weighted cross-entropy (weights from the training pixels), early stopping on the validation fold, 3 seeds (42, 1042, 2042) per round; the out-of-fold prediction is the mean probability of the seeds. Settings per experiment are on its page; the shared settings are on the experiment plan.

docs.title: 4. Fairness rules
docs.text:
flowchart LR subgraph SAME["Identical for every model"] P1["same labelled pixels"] P2["same tile store<br/>(composites, cloud mask, months)"] P3["same folds<br/>and rotation"] P4["same metrics and<br/>bootstrap draws"] end SAME --> D["only the model<br/>(or the one setting the<br/>experiment varies) differs"] D --> C["paired difference<br/>with 95% CI"]
  1. Every fitted step (normalisation statistics, class weights, early stopping) uses the training folds (early stopping: the validation fold); the test fold is used once, for the prediction.
  2. All inputs come from the same tile store.
  3. Models are compared on the same out-of-fold pixels with the same bootstrap draws.
  4. An experiment varies one thing against the experiment it builds on and states it.

docs.title: 5. Metrics and uncertainty
docs.text:
Metric Role Macro-F1 headline: mean F1 of irrigated and rainfed over the labelled pixels Rainfed F1, precision, recall the minority class: how many rainfed pixels are found (recall) and how many pixels predicted rainfed are rainfed (precision); the same three scores are kept for irrigated Overall accuracy for comparison with the literature only (dominated by the irrigated majority) Confusion matrix which way the errors go (rainfed → irrigated or irrigated → rainfed)

The kappa coefficient is not reported (Pontius & Millones 2011). Results are also given per region, per year (Morocco) and per zone.

95% confidence intervals: block bootstrap (Künsch 1989). The 20 km blocks, not the pixels, are the independent units. Each of 1,000 draws resamples whole blocks with replacement and recomputes the metric from the summed confusion matrices; the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles give the interval. The same draws are used for every run, so a difference between two models is measured on identical resamples (paired; Foody 2009).

docs.title: 6. How a result is read
docs.text:
• Δ = model − reference on the same pixels (references: E01 random forest and E03 U-TAE for E01–E04; within E05 the strategies against each other).
  • A model is better (or worse) only if the 95% CI of Δ excludes 0 and the Holm-adjusted p-value is below 0.05 (Holm 1979; correction over all comparisons of a table and metric).
  • A CI that excludes 0 without surviving Holm is reported as "higher / lower, not significant after Holm".
  • Otherwise: no clear difference. With few large blocks per fold, wide CIs are expected.
  • The paired tests are run for the headline macro-F1 and for the rainfed F1.

docs.title: 7. Reporting standard
docs.text: Every experiment has one page (docs/experiments/E0<N>_<name>.md) with the question, what changes from the previous experiment, the set-up, how to run it, and, once run, the results with confidence intervals, figures, the paired tests and an interpretation. The comparison table and paired tests of E01–E04 come from pixelwise_run/05_compare_experiments.py; E05 has its own report.py. Finished results are summarised on the Results page.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Foody, G. M. (2009). Classification accuracy comparison: hypothesis tests and the use of confidence intervals in evaluations of difference, equivalence and non-inferiority. Remote Sensing of Environment 113, 1658–1663.
  • Garnot, V. S. F., & Landrieu, L. (2021). Panoptic segmentation of satellite image time series with convolutional temporal attention networks. ICCV. https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07933
  • Holm, S. (1979). A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics 6, 65–70.
  • Kattenborn, T., et al. (2022). Spatially autocorrelated training and validation samples inflate performance assessment of convolutional neural networks. ISPRS Open Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing 5, 100018.
  • Künsch, H. R. (1989). The jackknife and the bootstrap for general stationary observations. Annals of Statistics 17, 1217–1241.
  • Ploton, P., et al. (2020). Spatial validation reveals poor predictive performance of large-scale ecological mapping models. Nature Communications 11, 4540.
  • Pontius, R. G., & Millones, M. (2011). Death to Kappa. International Journal of Remote Sensing 32, 4407–4429.
  • Roberts, D. R., et al. (2017). Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. Ecography 40, 913–929.
  • Varma, S., & Simon, R. (2006). Bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for model selection. BMC Bioinformatics 7, 91.

docs.title: RQ1 · Experiment plan
docs.text:
Research question RQ1: how accurately do geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) separate irrigated from rainfed pixels, compared with conventional classifiers trained on Sentinel-2 time series?

RQ1 is answered by the pixel-wise experiments E01–E04, Morocco first and Utah afterwards. The settings shared by every experiment (samples, classes, folds, metrics, statistical tests) are on the pixel-wise experiment plan; this page shows how the experiments answer RQ1 and where they stand. The earlier parcel-wise plan is kept in the archive.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
Every model classifies the 10 m pixels of the surveyed parcels into irrigated and rainfed (D16, D19) from the same 12 monthly Sentinel-2 composites (D14) and is scored on the same out-of-fold pixels, so every pair of models can be compared on identical pixels.

flowchart LR S["Labelled pixels (irrigated, rainfed)<br/>Morocco 2023/24 + 2024/25 first<br/>Utah 2023/24 later"] --> P["Pixel time series<br/>12 months × 12 bands"] S --> T["128 px tiles<br/>12 months"] P --> E01["E01 · random forest,<br/>gradient boosting"] P --> E02["E02 · TempCNN"] T --> E03["E03 · U-TAE<br/>from scratch"] T --> E04["E04 · frozen GeoFM<br/>+ L-TAE + UPerNet"] E01 --> C["Same out-of-fold pixels →<br/>paired block-bootstrap tests"] E02 --> C E04 --> C E03 --> C Question Comparison Experiments Q1 · Do frozen GeoFMs beat a classifier on the raw Sentinel-2 time series? each GeoFM vs the random forest E04 vs E01 Q2 · Do they beat a neural network trained from scratch on the same tiles? each GeoFM vs U-TAE E04 vs E03 Q3 · Does a temporal neural network beat the random forest on the same pixels? TempCNN vs random forest E02 vs E01 Q4 · Which GeoFM family works best: image models or pixel time-series models? Prithvi, Clay, TerraMind, AgriFM vs Presto, TESSERA within E04 Q5 · Do the conclusions hold in a second region? every question in Morocco and in Utah all

Headline metric: macro-F1 (mean F1 of irrigated and rainfed); a difference counts when its 95% block-bootstrap CI excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p < 0.05 (evaluation protocol).

docs.title: Experiments and status
docs.text:
ID Model Status E01 random forest, gradient boosting on the pixel time series planned (Morocco first) E02 TempCNN on the pixel time series planned (Morocco first) E03 U-TAE from scratch planned (Morocco first) E04 frozen Prithvi, Clay, TerraMind, AgriFM, Presto, TESSERA + L-TAE + UPerNet planned (Morocco first)

All runs side by side with the paired tests, once finished: comparison of the experiments.

docs.title: Remaining work for RQ1
docs.text:
1. Run E01–E04 for Morocco; comparison table and paired tests (pixelwise_run/05_compare_experiments.py).
  2. The same for Utah.
  3. Label efficiency: whether GeoFMs need fewer labels is tested in E05 for Prithvi (10–100% of the training parcels); extending it to the other models is an optional ablation (experiment plan §4).
  4. Write-up of RQ1 from E01–E04.

Fine-tuning (frozen vs LoRA vs full fine-tuning vs from scratch) belongs to RQ2: RQ2 · Fine-tuning.

docs.title: RQ2 · Fine-tuning and mapping model
docs.text: Research question RQ2: to what extent does fine-tuning a geospatial foundation model (GeoFM) improve on the frozen encoder, and how does the answer depend on the number of labelled parcels?

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
The earlier frozen-encoder benchmark (archived) pooled embeddings over parcel polygons and cannot produce wall-to-wall maps. All experiments therefore use pixel-level models, which serve both as the comparison and as the mapping model of Phase 5 (decision D11).

Component Description Where Frozen encoder + segmentation head each GeoFM with an L-TAE over the months and a UPerNet head trained on the labelled pixels of the tiles, as in PANGAEA E04 Fine-tuning and training from scratch Prithvi-EO-2.0 with the same head: frozen, LoRA (low-rank adapters), fully fine-tuned, or trained from random weights, with 10, 25, 50 or 100% of the training parcels E05 Classical baseline random forest and gradient boosting on the per-pixel Sentinel-2 time series E01 Neural baselines TempCNN (pixel time series; the pixel L-TAE is on hold), U-TAE (image time series), trained from scratch E02, E03

Training, tuning and testing follow the evaluation protocol: the same spatial folds and the PASTIS rotation, and the same out-of-fold pixels for every model (experiment plan). The task has two classes, irrigated and rainfed, on the labelled pixels of the surveyed parcels. E05 runs in Morocco first (2023/24 and 2024/25 pooled); Utah follows with the same plan.

docs.title: What fine-tuning means
docs.text:
A GeoFM is pretrained once, without labels, on very large amounts of imagery. Its encoder turns an image into features. For a task such as irrigated / rainfed mapping, a small head is added that turns the features into classes, and the head is trained on the labelled pixels.

Adapting the model means deciding which weights change during this training with labels: only the head, every weight, some of them, or a few new ones added to the encoder. The more weights change, the more the model can fit the new task, but the more labels and GPU memory it needs and the higher the risk of overfitting or of overwriting what was learnt in pretraining.

docs.title: Six ways to adapt a pretrained encoder
docs.text:
Grey: pretrained weights left unchanged. Orange: weights trained with the labels. Blue: small modules added to the encoder and trained with the labels. Green: weights trained without labels. Blocks drawn: 6 (Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M has 24).

The same, one strategy at a time (animation)

Strategy Trained Trained weights (Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M) Labels and memory needed Main risk 1 Frozen encoder + head (linear probe, or a decoder such as UPerNet) head only ≈ 2.5 M (our head) lowest features do not fit the task 2 Full fine-tuning every weight ≈ 306 M highest overfitting; pretrained features overwritten 3 Partial fine-tuning some encoder blocks + head between 1 and 2 medium choosing the right blocks 4 Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT): LoRA, adapters, prompt tuning, BitFit small added or selected weights + head ≈ 1–20 M (0.3–7% of the encoder) low less flexible than full fine-tuning 5 Linear probe, then fine-tune (LP-FT) stage 1 head, stage 2 every weight as 2 as 2 as 2, but milder 6 Continued self-supervised pretraining on unlabelled imagery of the region, then 1–5 encoder (or adapters) without labels, then as chosen as chosen unlabelled imagery and a pretraining run cost

1 · Frozen encoder + head. The encoder is used as a fixed feature extractor; only the head learns. A linear probe is the smallest head (one linear layer, Alain & Bengio 2016); in segmentation a decoder such as UPerNet is common (PANGAEA). Embeddings as data is the extreme case: the features are computed once and any classifier is trained on them (TESSERA, AlphaEarth). Cheap, hard to overfit, and a direct test of what pretraining learnt; but if the task needs features the encoder never learnt, the head cannot create them. This is E04 and the "frozen" run of E05.

2 · Full fine-tuning. Every encoder and head weight is trained, starting from the pretrained weights. It can adapt the features to the task, so it usually wins when there are enough labels, but it needs gradients and optimiser states for all ≈ 304 M encoder weights and can overfit small datasets. Two safeguards are standard:

  • discriminative learning rates: a smaller learning rate for the encoder than for the head (Howard & Ruder 2018), or layer-wise learning-rate decay, where each earlier block gets a smaller rate;
  • warm-up and gradient clipping, so that the large, noisy gradients of a still-random head do not damage the encoder in the first steps.

This is the "finetune" run of E05: encoder 10⁻⁵, head 10⁻⁴, 1 epoch of warm-up, gradient clipping at 1.0.

3 · Partial ("surgical") fine-tuning. Only some blocks are trained and the rest stay frozen. Training the upper blocks adapts the high-level features; training the first blocks suits a change in the input itself (a new sensor, resolution or band set). Lee et al. (2023) showed that the best choice depends on the kind of shift and can beat full fine-tuning.

4 · Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). The encoder stays frozen and a small number of weights are added or selected and trained with the head:

  • LoRA (low-rank adaptation; Hu et al. 2021): a low-rank update B·A next to a frozen weight matrix (see below);
  • adapters (Houlsby et al. 2019): small bottleneck MLPs inserted in each block;
  • visual prompt tuning (VPT; Jia et al. 2022): learnable extra tokens fed to the blocks with the image tokens;
  • BitFit (Ben Zaken et al. 2022): only the bias terms are trained.

The model keeps most of its pretrained knowledge while adapting; memory is close to the frozen case, and each task stores only a small file. Xin et al. (2024) review the vision methods.

5 · Linear probe, then fine-tune (LP-FT). First the head is trained on the frozen encoder (strategy 1), then every weight is fine-tuned starting from that trained head (strategy 2). Kumar et al. (2022) showed why this helps: with a random head, the first fine-tuning steps change the encoder to fit an arbitrary head and distort the pretrained features; starting from a good head avoids that.

6 · Continued self-supervised pretraining. Before using any labels, the encoder (or only adapters added to it) is pretrained further on unlabelled imagery of the target region or sensor with the original self-supervised task, for example masked-patch reconstruction. It brings the features closer to the target data, and then any of strategies 1–5 follows (Mendieta et al. 2023; Scheibenreif et al. 2024).

docs.title: LoRA in detail
docs.text: A linear layer computes W x with a pretrained matrix W (in Prithvi's attention, 1024 → 3072 values). LoRA keeps W frozen and adds a second path through two small matrices, A (r × 1024) and B (3072 × r), with a small rank r. Only A and B are trained. B starts at zero, so training starts exactly from the pretrained model; after training, B·A can be added into W, so the model is as fast as before. In E05, LoRA has rank 16 on the qkv projection and the two MLP layers (fc1, fc2) of every Prithvi block: 24 × (65,536 + 81,920 + 81,920) ≈ 5.5 M weights, about 1.8% of the encoder (Marti-Escofet et al. 2025).

docs.title: What this research does
docs.text:
flowchart TD A["E04 · frozen encoders + L-TAE + UPerNet<br/>(strategy 1, six GeoFMs)"] --> B["E05 · Prithvi frozen vs LoRA vs fully fine-tuned vs from scratch<br/>10 / 25 / 50 / 100% of the training parcels, Morocco first<br/>(strategies 1, 4 and 2)"] B --> C{"Does fine-tuning (LoRA or full) beat the frozen encoder<br/>(paired CI excludes 0 and Holm p below 0.05)?"} C -- "yes" --> D["Cheapest strategy that keeps the gain<br/>(LoRA if it matches full fine-tuning);<br/>optional LP-FT (5)"] C -- "no, or only with many labels" --> E["Frozen encoder for the maps;<br/>fine-tuning not needed"] D --> F["Best model → temporal and spatial test (Phase 3) → annual maps (Phase 5)"] E --> F
  • E05 measures the two ends and the middle: strategy 1 (frozen), strategy 4 (LoRA) and strategy 2 (full fine-tuning), plus the same network from random weights, which separates the value of pretraining (fine-tuned vs from scratch) from the value of training the encoder (fine-tuned vs frozen), and shows whether a small adaptation (LoRA vs full fine-tuning) is enough.
  • The label shares (10–100%) test the claim of several studies that pretraining matters most when labels are few.
  • LoRA runs after the other three strategies (same jobs, later). LP-FT (5) is optional, if E05 shows a gain from training the encoder. Continued pretraining (6) is left out: it needs a pretraining run per region.
  • In E05, "fine-tuned" means full fine-tuning with discriminative learning rates; the LoRA runs are named separately ("LoRA": rank 16, α 32, on the qkv, fc1 and fc2 layers, 5.5 M adapter weights).

docs.title: Papers to read
docs.text: Six papers, in reading order. Each one adapts a pretrained model differently; together they cover the strategies above and the evidence for and against fine-tuning GeoFMs.

docs.title: 1 · Tomotaki-Dawoud et al. (2025) — Prithvi frozen vs fully fine-tuned vs from scratch
docs.text:
Fine-tuning the Prithvi foundation model for crop-type and health mapping in smallholder farms. Procedia Computer Science 270. Summary page.

  • Their fine-tuning: strategies 1 and 2 with Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M and a segmentation decoder, plus training from scratch; one learning rate (10⁻⁴) for all weights, 100 epochs; 20–100% of the training data.
  • Finding: full fine-tuning best for crop type (macro-F1 0.79 vs 0.56 frozen and 0.63 from scratch), with the largest gain over training from scratch at 20–40% of the data; overfitting on the imbalanced crop-health task.
  • Why read it: the direct model for E05. Its 601 parcels, single split and 30 m imagery upsampled to 0.5 m make the result a hypothesis to test rather than firm evidence.

docs.title: 2 · Marti-Escofet et al. (2025) — PEFT for GeoFMs
docs.text:
Fine-tune smarter, not harder: parameter-efficient fine-tuning for geospatial foundation models. arXiv:2504.17397.

  • Their fine-tuning: strategies 1, 2 and 4 compared on Prithvi 1.0 and 2.0, Clay and DeCUR, five segmentation datasets (floods, burn scars, land cover, cashew plantations, South African crop types), 5 seeds each; LoRA with rank 16 on the attention query and value and the feed-forward layers, VPT with 100 prompts, ViT adapter.
  • Finding: for Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M, LoRA (5.5 M weights, 1.8% of the encoder) matched full fine-tuning on average (test mIoU 68.02 vs 68.14), and both were far above the linear probe (51.55). On held-out regions LoRA generalised better (floods: 87.57 vs 82.07). For Clay, LoRA stayed below full fine-tuning. Among decoders, UNet did best and UPerNet worst in most settings.
  • Why read it: the closest study to the LoRA run of E05 (same encoder, same LoRA set-up), from the authors of TerraTorch; the decoder result is relevant to the UPerNet head used here.

docs.title: 3 · Kumar et al. (2022) — why full fine-tuning can hurt (LP-FT)
docs.text:
Fine-tuning can distort pretrained features and underperform out-of-distribution. ICLR 2022. arXiv:2202.10054.

  • Their fine-tuning: strategies 1, 2 and 5 on 10 datasets with a distribution shift between training and test.
  • Finding: full fine-tuning was about 2% better than linear probing on data like the training data but about 7% worse out of distribution; LP-FT was about 1% better than full fine-tuning on the former and about 10% better on the latter.
  • Why read it: the explanation of feature distortion behind the warm-up and small encoder learning rate of E05; relevant to RQ3 and RQ4, where the test year or region differs from training.

docs.title: 4 · Hu et al. (2021) — LoRA
docs.text:
LoRA: low-rank adaptation of large language models. arXiv:2106.09685.

  • Their fine-tuning: strategy 4: frozen weights plus trainable low-rank updates B·A in the attention layers of language models (RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, GPT-3).
  • Finding: on par with or better than full fine-tuning; for GPT-3 175B, 10,000 times fewer trained weights and 3 times less GPU memory, and no extra cost at inference.
  • Why read it: the method itself (rank, scaling α/r, zero start of B), implemented in add_lora.

docs.title: 5 · Scheibenreif, Mommert & Borth (2024) — self-supervised adaptation with low-rank adapters
docs.text:
Parameter efficient self-supervised geospatial domain adaptation. CVPR 2024, 27841–27851. Paper.

  • Their fine-tuning: strategies 6 + 4: scaled low-rank (SLR) adapters (a LoRA-like low-rank path plus two learnable scaling vectors) are added to the attention and MLP layers of ViT-L models (MAE, SatMAE, Scale-MAE); they are first trained with masked autoencoding on unlabelled target-domain images, then the model is evaluated with a linear head or fine-tuned on 8 remote sensing datasets (optical, multispectral, SAR).
  • Finding: linear-evaluation accuracy up 4–6 points and few-shot accuracy up 6–10 points; better than full fine-tuning while training 1–2% of the weights.
  • Why read it: the cheapest way to adapt a GeoFM to a new region or sensor without labels.

docs.title: 6 · Feng et al. (2025) — TESSERA: no gain from fine-tuning
docs.text:
TESSERA: temporal embeddings of surface spectra for Earth representation and analysis. arXiv:2506.20380. Summary page.

  • Their fine-tuning: strategy 1 (frozen embeddings with small heads) as the main use; ablations with full fine-tuning of the encoder at three learning-rate settings, and with random weights.
  • Finding: fine-tuning gave no gain over the frozen embeddings, while pretraining itself was worth 33.5 F1 points (crop classification, Austria).
  • Why read it: the counter-example to paper 1. For a pixel time-series model with a strong pretraining objective, the frozen encoder was enough.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
• LoRA rank and target layers: E05 follows Marti-Escofet et al. (2025) (rank 16 on attention and feed-forward layers); no search over the rank.
  • Decoder: UPerNet in E03–E05 (as PANGAEA); Marti-Escofet et al. (2025) found a UNet decoder better for fine-tuned GeoFMs.
  • Aggregation of the pixel predictions to parcels for a comparison with the archived parcel-wise results.

docs.title: Phase 2 · Model evaluation
docs.text:
Phase 2 compares geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) and ways of adapting them for classifying every 10 m pixel of the surveyed parcels as irrigated or rainfed (D16). All surveyed parcels are cropland, so no cropland mask is used here (D19); the cropland extent is a question of the mapping phase (Phase 5). All experiments run in Morocco first (2023/24 and 2024/25 pooled); Utah follows later with the same plan (D13). The phase answers two research questions under one evaluation protocol; every model is scored on the same out-of-fold pixels.

RQ Question Experiments Status Page RQ1 How accurately do frozen GeoFMs classify the pixels, compared with classifiers trained on the Sentinel-2 time series and a network trained from scratch? E01–E04 📝 planned, Morocco first RQ1 · Experiment plan RQ2 To what extent does fine-tuning (LoRA or full) improve on the frozen encoder and on training from scratch, and how does this depend on the number of labelled parcels? E05 (Prithvi) 📝 planned, Morocco first RQ2 · Fine-tuning

docs.title: Phase 3 · Temporal and spatial transferability
docs.text:
Starter page

Planned for February – March 2027. This page will be extended into an overview and component pages when the work begins.

Objective 2: evaluate the temporal transferability of the models of Phase 2 and whether their results hold in a second, independent region (Utah).

RQ Question Planned test RQ3 (temporal) How temporally consistent is the best model across years? Utah: train on WRLU 2024, test on WRLU 2021 on the folds held out in training (same fields, paired); Morocco: year-to-year consistency of the annual maps RQ4 (second region) Do the results of Morocco hold in a second, independent region? the Phase 2 experiments (E01–E05) run in Morocco first and then in Utah with the same plan, each region with its own labels and spatial folds (D13); no Morocco → Utah transfer

docs.title: Decided
docs.text:
• Second region and temporal test: Utah (D13); dataset: Utah training data. The temporal test holds out space as well, because the WRLU labels barely change between years.
  • Metrics: macro-F1 of irrigated and rainfed, and rainfed F1, per region as in Phase 2; temporal: the drop from WRLU 2024 (score A) to WRLU 2021 (score B) on the same held-out fields.

docs.text: • Wording of RQ3 / RQ4 in the report, to be agreed with the supervisors (departure from the proposal).

docs.title: Phase 4 · Multi-model fusion
docs.text:
Starter page

Optional extension, planned for December 2026 – January 2027 if time allows.

Research question RQ5: does fusing the features or outputs of several foundation models improve on the best single model?

docs.title: Candidate strategies
docs.text:
Strategy Description Early fusion concatenation of the pixel / patch features of several frozen encoders (E04) before the decoder Late fusion combination of the per-pixel class probabilities of the single-model runs (averaging or stacking) Learned fusion a small network that weights the features of the encoders, trained under the same protocol

All strategies are compared with the best single model of Phase 2 on the same out-of-fold pixels, folds and bootstrap samples (evaluation protocol). The complementarity of the models (different pretraining data and objectives, e.g. AgriFM with its temporal design) motivates the comparison. All inputs are Sentinel-2 only (D14).

docs.title: Phase 5 · Annual irrigated-cropland maps
docs.text:
Starter page

Planned for March 2027. This page will be extended when the mapping work begins.

Aim: produce annual 10 m maps of irrigated and rainfed cropland for Morocco (2021–2025) and for Utah, the second study area (D13), using the best model of Phases 2–4, and assess them against independent data.

docs.title: Planned workflow
docs.text: Step Description Imagery 12 monthly Sentinel-2 composites per agricultural year for every 128 px tile with ≥ 1% cropland, from the STAC download s2_download/ (Phase 1, Cropland extent and mask §5); Sentinel-2 only (D14) Cropland mask to be decided in this phase (D19). The experiments classify only the surveyed parcels (irrigated or rainfed) and use no mask, so where the maps are made is chosen here. Candidates: the union of four cropland products per agricultural year (D17, cropland_extent/make_cropland_mask.py), stricter variants (e.g. ≥ 2 votes), and Dynamic World alone (cropland_extent/download_dynamic_world.py: annual most frequent class, mean crop probability). They are compared on their omission of the surveyed irrigated and rainfed parcels and on their commission (land in the mask that is not cropland) (Cropland extent and mask) Land that is not cropland to be decided in this phase: handled by the mask alone, or by an extra "not cropland" class added to the mapping model; predictions are kept inside the chosen mask Inference the best model of the experiments E01–E05 (Experiments), applied tile by tile Accuracy assessment a stratified random sample over the map (including land outside the mask and not cropland), area-adjusted accuracy and area estimates with confidence intervals (Olofsson et al. 2014; experiment plan §3); the GMIA-NEXT reference points as an independent comparison Comparison national statistics (FAO AQUASTAT) and existing products (LGRIP30, GMIE, WorldCereal)

docs.text:
• annual irrigated-cropland maps, Morocco, 2021–2025, 10 m;
  • annual maps of Utah;

docs.title: Heads and mapping: what GeoFM crop studies use
docs.text:
Literature search of 6 Nov 2026: which head is put on a GeoFM for crop classification, which neural baselines are used, and what wall-to-wall mapping requires. Result: decision D11, since superseded by D16 (every model is pixel-wise).

Head Used for Papers Classical ML on frozen embeddings (LogReg, RF, GBDT, SVM, kNN) per-pixel / per-parcel classification Presto (Tseng et al. 2023); AlphaEarth irrigated vs rainfed (Yang et al. 2026); AlphaEarth cropland maps (Mughees et al. 2026); Galileo / CropFM + RF (Nedungadi et al. 2026) Small neural head (linear, MLP) per-pixel classification, fine-tuning TESSERA, 2-layer MLP per pixel (Feng et al. 2025); Presto / AlphaEarth + RF or MLP (Tong & Wang 2025); WorldCereal, fine-tuned Presto (Butsko et al. 2025) Segmentation decoder (UPerNet, UNet) wall-to-wall maps from patch-based models PANGAEA (Marsocci et al. 2024); Prithvi-EO-2.0 (Szwarcman et al. 2024) Neural baseline (from scratch) Input Gives maps Note TempCNN (Pelletier et al. 2019) pixel time series yes, per pixel 1D-CNN > RF for irrigated mapping (Bazzi et al. 2019); TempCNN-type models transfer better across regions than GeoFM embeddings (Tong & Wang 2025) L-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2020) pixel or parcel time series yes temporal head of E04 / E05 (a pixel L-TAE in E02 is on hold) U-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2021) image tiles yes, 10 m PASTIS baseline; counterpart of GeoFM + UPerNet (E03) PSE-TAE (Garnot et al. 2020) parcel pixel sets no (needs polygons) parcel-level only (archived parcel-wise baseline) LSTM, Transformer (BreizhCrops, Rußwurm et al. 2020) pixel time series yes similar to TempCNN in benchmarks

Main points - Several 2025–26 studies find the head choice matters little on frozen embeddings (LogReg within 0.3 pp of a boosted ensemble, Mughees et al. 2026). In the archived parcel-wise E01, RF was weaker on dense PCA embeddings. The current pixel-wise design uses one head for every GeoFM (L-TAE + UPerNet, E04) (D16). - GeoFM embeddings degrade under large geographic shifts (cross-continent) more than simple temporal CNNs (Tong & Wang 2025): relevant when the conclusions are compared between Morocco and Utah (RQ4). - Fine-tuning helps in operational crop mapping (WorldCereal) but can collapse pretrained features without care (Nedungadi et al. 2026): relevant for RQ2.
